transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-06
Start: 10:00 PDT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Dave Huang (Acme ML ML Eng), Priya Nair (Acme Infra Eng), Sarah Kim (Acme Product), Tom Alvarez (CTO, joined 10:25)

Summary:
Quick POC weekly sync focused on cost/unit economics. Reviewed recent benchmark runs, caching and batching tradeoffs, and prioritized next steps: deeper benchmarks with varied batch sizes and KV-cache on/off, updated cost model to send, and a follow-up quantization/deep-dive.

Topics:
- Baseline throughput and cost metrics (tokens/sec/$)
- Caching savings from prefix/KV cache for repeated prompts
- Batching tradeoffs: throughput vs latency impact
- Quantization impact and quality tradeoffs
- Next steps for pilot to estimate production unit economics

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: awesome, hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh quick check, can everyone hear me?
[00:03] Dave: yeah, can hear you Jordan.
[00:05] Priya: good here.
[00:07] Jordan: great, so today we'll focus mostly on the cost numbers, tokens per second per dollar, and how caching and batching change the economics. Maya and I ran the benchmark cluster yesterday and brought some numbers.
[00:22] Maya: yeah I'll start - quick caveat, these are synthetic-ish runs using your prompt distribution but not full production traces until you share them, but we did token lengths 64/256/1024 to match what Sarah sent.
[00:35] Sarah: yep that's the distribution we care about.
[00:37] Maya: baseline, single-node run, batch size 1, no KV cache, 256 tokens median: about 1,400 tokens/sec per dollar. With batch size 4 that goes to ~3,600 tokens/sec/$, and batch size 8 to about 4,900 tokens/sec/$. So batching gives 2.5-3.5x throughput improvements.
[01:00] Dave: can you explain the tokens/sec/$ unit again? just to be clear how to map to our cost per 1M tokens?
[01:06] Jordan: sure - think of tokens/sec/$ as throughput-normalized by cost: if an instance costs $X/hr and you get Y tokens/sec, you can convert to cost per 1M tokens easily. we included a pricing workbook but we'll send the updated one with per-instance numbers.
[01:20] Priya: ok, what about latency? our app needs sub-250ms median tail for interactive flows.
[01:26] Maya: right, so tradeoff: batch size 8 improved throughput but increased median latency from ~140ms at batch 1 to ~360ms at batch 8 in our config. So for sub-250ms target we recommend staying at batch 4 or using dynamic batching with a 120ms timeout to avoid tail bloat.
[01:44] Sarah: is there a way to get batching efficiency without hurting median latency?
[01:49] Maya: two levers - dynamic batching (time window + max batch) and prefix/KV caching to reduce work per request. If a lot of your requests share prefixes we see big wins with KV caching.
[01:58] Dave: how big were the caching savings? numbers?
[02:00] Maya: in our runs with your 30% prefix overlap case, KV caching saved about 28% tokens served and gave ~22% cost reduction overall. In a higher overlap synthetic (~50% shared prefix) savings were 40% tokens served and ~33% cost reduction.
[02:18] Priya: that's promising, but we have concerns about KV cache memory footprint and eviction - how is that managed?
[02:25] Maya: cache is sharded per model instance, LRU-ish eviction, and we provide tooling to estimate memory given avg prefix length and user concurrency. we'll share the calculator. also note on private/dedicated, you can pin instances to keep warm caches for stateful flows.
[02:40] Tom (joined): hey sorry late, do we have an estimate of end-to-end cost per 1M tokens for our typical mix?
[02:46] Jordan: rough from yesterday's runs: with batch 4 + cache on, quantized int8 model, estimate ~$0.16 per 1k tokens, so roughly $160 per 1M tokens. With batch 1 and no cache it's more like $360 per 1M tokens. Those are ballpark - we'll send a cleaned workbook with per-instance and sensitivity bands.
[03:08] Dave: quantization was int8? any quality regressions?
[03:11] Maya: we used an int8-aware quant for this run with calibration; quality delta on your evalset was minor - about 0.7% relative drop on BLEU-ish metric you shared. but we'll run more evals; for some prompts we saw artifacts so we'd want a targeted quality review before recommending int8 for all routes.
[03:29] Sarah: could we do hybrid: int8 for bulk low-criticality calls and fp16 for high-quality endpoints?
[03:34] Maya: yes that's a common pattern - route by priority and have fallback rules; Redwood supports automatic fallback to higher-precision variants if quality checks fail or latency SLOs allow.
[03:44] Priya: any notes on VPC/private deployment differences for cost? e.g. network overhead or data egress costs?
[03:50] Jordan: on private infra you generally pay instance cost but avoid data egress to hosted; networking can add small overhead but it's predictable. for dedicated we provide SLA and optimized kernel builds to squeeze more throughput, which lowers tokens/sec/$ versus generic cloud endpoints.
[04:06] Dave: curious about tail latency percentiles - p95/p99?
[04:09] Maya: p95 with batch 4 was ~420ms, p99 was closer to 1s in our noisy runs - that's why dynamic batching with timeout and per-route SLOs are important. You can also pre-warm KV caches for hottest keys.
[04:25] Sarah: ok, so actionables?
[04:27] Jordan: quick recap - Maya will run a 3-run benchmark matrix with batch sizes 1/4/8, cache on/off, and quantization variants (fp16/int8), then produce a short table with tokens/sec/$, median/p95 latencies, and cost per 1M tokens. Dave will send anonymized traces so Maya can run with real distributions. I'll email pricing workbook and examples of caching configs. we'll also schedule a 45m quantization deep dive next week.
[04:52] Tom: sounds good. one quick ask - can you include a small section in the workbook showing how routing policies (dedicated vs hosted fallback) change expected cost if we hit peak traffic?
[05:01] Jordan: yes, we'll add a routing sensitivity tab.
[05:04] Maya: last note - for the pilot if you keep critical paths at batch 1 but enable KV cache you might get most of the cost benefit without violating your median latency SLO.
[05:13] Dave: nice. thanks.
[05:15] Jordan: ok we'll wrap - thanks everyone, sending notes and items after call.

End of transcript.
